title: Hindi Journalism Must Act as an Effective Bridge in the Journey of Schemes 'From File to Field'
subtitle:
Not Just Translation, the Spirit and Objective of Government Schemes Must Reach the Public: Sudha Shrimali

Hindi and Digital Media Have a Key Role in Connecting the Resolve of 'Viksit Bharat 2047' with Public Participation
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                28 SEP 2026 6:18PM by PIB Raipur
content:
After the announcement of any government scheme, its real impact begins when information about it reaches the intended beneficiary. Translating the complex language of a scheme into simple language easily understood by the common man, and delivering it in the correct context, is the vital link that completes the journey of government schemes "from file to field." Hindi journalism can play the role of an effective bridge in this process. These views were expressed by Ms. Sudha Shrimali, Business Editor of Navbharat Times, during a special lecture organized on the occasion of Hindi Month.
At the beginning of the program, Additional Director General Shri Siddharth Bodke welcomed Ms. Sudha Shrimali and felicitated her for the special lecture.
Speaking on the topic "Role of Hindi Journalism in Taking Government Schemes to the Masses – In the Context of Viksit Bharat 2047", Ms. Shrimali stated that presenting government information in Hindi is not merely a task of translating words. It is far more important to understand the objective, spirit, and context behind the information and present it according to the needs of the public. When accurate information reaches people in a simple and useful format, it ceases to be mere information and becomes a driver of public participation.
Ms. Shrimali noted that whenever a scheme is announced, basic questions arise in the mind of an ordinary citizen—what is the scheme, who will benefit from it, what are the eligibility criteria, and how can one avail of the benefits? The responsibility of journalism is to provide direct and clear answers to these questions. Citing examples like the Prime Minister Street Vendor’s AtmaNirbhar Nidhi (PM SVANidhi) scheme, she stated that the headline and presentation of news should be such that a reader can understand at a single glance why the scheme is relevant to them and how they can benefit from it.
She added that the world of information is evolving rapidly today. Alongside newspapers, audio programming, social media, and other digital platforms have developed the capacity to disseminate information on government policies and schemes far more widely than before. In such times, the foremost responsibility of the media is to maintain credibility. Simple, fact-based information can bridge the communication gap while minimizing the spread of rumors and misleading information.
She also emphasized that the flow of information should not be a one-way channel from the government to the media and then to the public. The role of the Press Information Bureau is equally crucial in conveying media feedback back to the government. Through queries, reactions, and ground-level insights gathered from journalists and media organizations, information gaps can be identified and addressed.
Regarding the role of journalism in the era of Artificial Intelligence, she remarked that instead of viewing AI strictly as a challenge, it should be embraced as an auxiliary tool that makes a journalist's work more effective. Technology can assist in information analysis, presentation, and wide distribution, but the ultimate responsibility for ensuring the truth and credibility of information will always rest on journalism.
Ms. Shrimali stated that while information on government schemes should be engaging and useful, its aim should not be to glorify schemes, but to convey their core intent and benefits to the public in simple language. The widespread understanding of Hindi and the expanding reach of digital media render this approach even more effective. From this perspective, Hindi Journalism can play a pivotal role in linking the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047 with a broad campaign of public participation.
Director General (West Zone), Press Information Bureau, Smt. Smita Vats Sharma, in her address, stated, "In today's digital era, there is an overload of information. Therefore, our continuous effort is to curate data and information for journalists and present it in an extremely simplified manner. For the convenience of journalists, we attach PIB backgrounders alongside press releases and write detailed captions for photographs so that journalists working in far-flung areas can easily grasp the background. Additionally, to ensure a comprehensive understanding of the topic, social media links and live-streaming links are also shared with the release."
This special lecture was organized by the Press Information Bureau, Mumbai, on the occasion of Hindi Month under the guidance of Director General Smt. Smita Vats Sharma. On this occasion, officers and staff from the Press Information Bureau and the Central Bureau of Communication across the zone joined the lecture online. At the conclusion of the event, Director, PIB Bhopal, Shri Manish Gautam, expressed his gratitude to Ms. Sudha Shrimali.

The Ministry of Mines, Government of India, is strengthening its E-Waste Collection Campaign under Special Campaign 6 with a focus on responsible e-waste management, resource recovery and promotion of a circular economy.
The campaign is being coordinated and implemented through the Jawaharlal Nehru Aluminium Research Development and Design Centre (JNARDDC), Nagpur, designated as the Nodal Agency for the campaign, in association with the Material Recycling Association of India (MRAI). E-waste is not merely a waste stream but also a potential source of valuable secondary resources. With several electronic products containing minerals and metals that are important for modern technologies, recycling and recovery from e-waste can contribute to resource efficiency and strengthen the circular economy for critical minerals. Responsible recycling can help recover valuable materials, reduce pressure on primary mineral resources and promote sustainable utilisation of resources.
As part of the preparatory activities for effective implementation of the campaign, JNARDDC has conducted virtual coordination meetings with designated Nodal Officers of various offices and organisations under the Ministry of Mines, including the Geological Survey of India (GSI), Indian Bureau of Mines (IBM), National Institute of Rock Mechanics (NIRM), National Aluminium Company Limited (NALCO), Hindustan Zinc Limited (HZL), Mineral Exploration and Consultancy Limited (MECL) and Hindustan Copper Limited (HCL).

These activities aim to promote awareness about responsible e-waste disposal and encourage reuse, repurposing and recycling of discarded electronic and electrical products, wherever feasible.
Through the campaign, the Ministry is promoting Jan Bhagidari in resource conservation and encouraging responsible practices for the collection, segregation, recycling and recovery of materials from e-waste. title: Indian Railways Approves ₹122 Crore for 6 km Barbil–Bolanikhadan Doubling Project of South Eastern Railway

date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                28 SEP 2026 5:32PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Indian Railways has approved the 6 km Barbil-Bolanikhadan Doubling Project of South Eastern Railway at a completion cost of ₹122 crore, strengthening rail infrastructure on an important mineral movement corridor.
Doubling to Support Growing Freight Traffic
The project will facilitate additional freight traffic of 8.9 MTPA on this stretch after commissioning of the project. The doubling will also help reduce delays to freight trains.
The Barbil-Bolanikhadan section has been identified under the “Energy, Mineral and Cement Corridor” of Indian Railways. The existing section is a single-line section and currently carries about 9 MTPA, comprising about 6 loaded rakes per day of originating iron ore traffic. The traffic is entirely for high-grade ore and pellets moving from SAIL’s Bolani mines and private sidings (Rungta, Khatau Narbheram) to major steel plants and ports.
Meeting Future Freight Requirements
Doubling this 6 km stretch, ahead of the full realisation of SAIL’s mine expansion and port/plant capacity additions, will help to prevent the capacity constraints in the designated mineral corridor.
The approved work will support the growing freight requirements, improve rail connectivity for movement of iron ore to steel plants and ports, and strengthen rail capacity as mining, industrial and port activities expand in the region. It will also strengthen the Energy, Mineral and Cement Corridor and support smoother movement of freight on this important route.

title: Quick Estimates of Index of Industrial Production and Use- Based Index for the Month of August 2026 (Base 2022-23=100)
subtitle:
India's Index of industrial production records growth of 8.0% in August 2026

In August 2026, Index of Industrial Production recorded an 8.0% year-on-year growth, supported by 9.0% growth in Manufacturing sector and strong growth of 12.3% in Electricity & Gas Supply sector.

In a record performance, manufacturing sector recorded growth of 8% or more in the last three consecutive months.
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                28 SEP 2026 4:00PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Quick Estimate of Index of Industrial Production (IIP) is released on 28th of every month (or next working day if 28th is a holiday). The index is compiled with data received from source agencies, which in turn receive the data from the producing factories/ establishments. These Quick Estimates will undergo revision in subsequent releases as per the revision policy of IIP.
2.  Key Highlights:
The IIP growth rate for the month of August 2026 is 8.0 percent which was 6.7 percent (Quick Estimate) in the month of July 2026.
The growth rates of the sectors, Mining & Quarrying, Manufacturing, Electricity & Gas Supply and Water Supply, Sewerage & Waste Management for the month of August 2026 are (-) 5.6 percent, 9.0 percent, 12.3 percent and 6.3 percent respectively.
The Quick Estimate of IIP stands at 123.3 against 114.2 in August 2025. The indices of Industrial Production for Mining & Quarrying, Manufacturing, Electricity & Gas Supply and Water Supply, Sewerage & Waste Management for the month of August 2026 stand at 85.7, 126.6, 133.9 and 147.6 respectively.
Within the Manufacturing sector, 18 out of 23 industry groups at NIC 2 digit-level have recorded a positive growth in August 2026 over August 2025. The top three positive contributors for the month of August 2026 are – “Manufacture of motor vehicles, trailers and semi-trailers” (25.2%), “Manufacture of electrical equipment” (30.9%), and “Manufacture of other transport equipment” (25.3%).
In the industry group “Manufacture of motor vehicles, trailers and semi-trailers” item groups “Auto Components, Spares and Accessories”, “Passenger Cars”, and “Commercial Vehicles” have shown significant contribution in growth.
In the industry group “Manufacture of electrical equipment”, item groups “Electrical Apparatus for Switching or Protecting Electrical Circuits (e.g., Switchgear, Circuit Breakers/Switches, Control/Meter Panels) and Parts Thereof”, “End-Face Connectors for Optical Fibres and Cables” and “UPS and Solid-State Drives” have shown significant contribution in growth.

As per the Use-Based Classification, the indices stand at 111.8 for Primary Goods, 140.7 for Capital Goods, 131.8 for Intermediate Goods and 132.5 for Infrastructure/ Construction Goods for the month of August 2026. title: Ministry of Steel Announces Apex Body for  Strengthening Safety Standards and improve safety culture in Steel sector
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                28 SEP 2026 6:10PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Ministry of Steel, Government of India, has decided to set up a
Steel Industry Safety Council (SISC)
as an apex-level industry safety body under the administrative control of the Ministry of Steel. The initiative is aimed at strengthening safety standards, practices, accident prevention and safety awareness across the steel industry.
The Council will be headed by the
Secretary, Ministry of Steel
, as Chairman and will include senior officials of the Ministry, Chief Executives of integrated steel producers, and representatives of key technical and statutory organisations including the
Directorate General of Mines Safety (DGMS), Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organisation (PESO), National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA)
and recognised steel technology institutions.
The SISC will assess the safety situation in the steel industry, facilitate studies and improvements in safety practices, approve industry safety standards and recommended practices, and review serious accidents, accidents and near-miss incidents. It will also provide directions for strengthening safety awareness, training and preventive measures.
To provide technical and professional support to the Council, a
Steel Industry Safety Directorate (SISD)
will be established. The Directorate will have expertise in areas including process safety, blast furnaces, steel melting, rolling mills, coke ovens, refractory systems, electrical and mechanical safety, occupational health, fire engineering and disaster management.
The SISD will oversee implementation of the Council's decisions, undertake periodic safety audits and reviews, maintain and disseminate accident and near-miss information, conduct investigations into serious safety incidents, review emergency preparedness and safety training programmes, and develop and issue
Steel Industry Safety Standards, Recommended Practices and Guidelines
suited to Indian conditions.
The establishment of SISC and SISD represents an important institutional step towards
promoting a stronger safety culture, improving prevention of industrial accidents and advancing consistent safety practices across India's steel industry
.

title: Green Highways
subtitle: India's Journey Towards Sustainable Road Infrastructure
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                28 SEP 2026 6:30PM by PIB Delhi
content:
India’s green highway approach is transforming road infrastructure through
plantation, climate-resilient design and resource-efficient construction
. Over the last five years,
more than 3.61 crore saplings
have been planted across approximately
1.32 lakh km of National Highways
.
From Miyawaki forests to recycled construction materials and indigenous bio-bitumen technology, green practices are shaping highway development. Satellite-based monitoring through the National Highways Green Cover Index is strengthening scientific assessment of green cover. Community initiatives and pollinator corridors are also adding a wider ecological dimension.
Building Roads, Growing Green
India’s highways are no longer just corridors of connectivity. They are becoming an important part of the country’s broader infrastructure transformation. As road infrastructure expands, the focus is also shifting towards building corridors that are efficient, resilient and environmentally responsible.
Over the past decade, India’s National Highway network has grown by nearly
61%
, from
91,287 km
in 2014 to
1,46,572 km
by March 2026. This rapid development has strengthened connectivity, improved access to markets and supported faster movement of people and goods. As road infrastructure expands, the focus is also shifting towards building corridors that are efficient, resilient and environmentally responsible. Large-scale plantation along National Highways (NH), the use of recycled and waste-derived materials, energy-efficient construction practices, and satellite-based monitoring of green cover are contributing to a more sustainable highway network.
Green Highways Policy, 2015: Policy Evolution
The greening of India’s National Highway network is guided by the
Green Highways (Plantation, Transplantation, Beautification and Maintenance) Policy, 2015
. The Policy was formulated to:
Evolve a policy framework for plantation along National Highways.
Reduce the impact of air pollution and dust, as trees and shrubs are known to be natural sinks for air pollutants.
Arrest soil erosion at the embankment slopes.
Moderate the effect of wind and incoming radiation.
Create employment opportunities for local people.
The implementation of the policy brings together multiple stakeholders. Plantation activities are undertaken by
Self Help Groups, private agencies, State Forest Departments, Forest Corporations and contractors
, according to the scope of sanctioned works. A
Plantation Cell
has been established for overall monitoring through regional offices of the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) and other agencies.
Greening the Corridors: Plantation & Afforestation
The greening of National Highways is increasingly being measured by the number of saplings planted, their survival, growth and distribution along highway corridors. As of July 2026, more than
3.61 crore saplings
have been planted across approximately
1.32 lakh km
of National Highways during the last five years. The approach has also expanded from plantation to broader environmental management. Earlier, monitoring of plantations relied primarily on site visits by field personnel. Today, this is being supplemented by
drone and satellite based monitoring.
Miyawaki plantations
have also been introduced to increase green cover. Wherever tree felling is necessary for highway development,
compensatory afforestation and tree transplantation
are being undertaken.
The Miyawaki technique is a method of creating dense forests within limited spaces. Also known as the
‘pot plantation method’
, it involves planting trees and shrubs close to one another to promote rapid growth and establish forest-like ecosystems in a shorter period. Plants can grow up to
10 times faster
under this method, making it particularly suitable for expanding green cover in space-constrained urban areas.
Plantation and landscaping have become an integral part of National Highway development and project completion. NHAI’s September 2026 guidelines reinforce this approach. Plantation works will be considered compliant for provisional completion certification only when at least 80% of the available
Right of Way (RoW)
earmarked for plantation has been covered. RoW refers to the designated land area that is legally required for the construction, operation, and maintenance of highway infrastructure. The planted saplings must also have a minimum 90% survival rate at the time of inspection by officials. The same survival benchmark applies during the Operations and Maintenance period, with provisions for timely replacement of plants that do not survive.
To encourage good practices, NHAI instituted the Green Highways Excellence Awards in 2025. The 2026 awards placed the highest weightage on plantation survival, along with species diversity, use of native species, site-specific plans and protection measures.
In the
Avenue Plantations
category, the Six-Laning of the Chilakaluripet Bypass on NH-16 in Andhra Pradesh secured the First Prize.
In the
Median Plantations
category, the Four-Laning of the Hyderabad–Yadgiri section of NH-163was awarded the First Prize.
The Jamtha Clover Leaf Oxygen Bird Park on NH-44,Nagpur, received the First Prize in the
Plantation in Land Parcels category.
These award-winning efforts show how every stretch of a highway can become an opportunity to add greenery and strengthen the surrounding landscape.
National Highways – Green Cover Index (NH-GCI)
Marking a new milestone in sustainable highway development, the first Annual Report on the
National Highways Green Cover Index (NH-GCI) 2025–26
has been released. Prepared in collaboration with the
National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC) of ISRO,
the report provides the country's
first scientific and quantitative assessment of green cover
within the RoW along National Highways. The assessment covers nearly
30,000 kilometres of National Highways
under the
Operation and Maintenance (O&M) phase
across 24 states. It includes observations recorded before and after the monsoon season. Using advanced space-based technologies, it establishes a reliable baseline for monitoring and enhancing roadside plantations. The assessment reveals significant variation in green cover along National Highways. The findings enable comparison, ranking, and targeted interventions for improved plantation management.
Driving the Shift to Sustainable Materials
India’s highways are also transitioning from fossil-fuel-based materials towards bio-based, regenerative solutions. A
major scientific breakthrough
was announced in January 2026 with the technology transfer of Bio-Bitumen produced via pyrolysis of farm residue. Technology transfer (TT) is a process that allows scientific findings, knowledge and intellectual property to flow from universities and research institutions to public and private users.
The innovation,
“Bio-Bitumen via Pyrolysis: From Farm Residue to Roads”,
was developed jointly by
CSIR-Central Road Research Institute (CSIR-CRRI), New Delhi
, and
CSIR-Indian Institute of Petroleum (CSIR-IIP), Dehradun.
Bitumen is a mixture of organic liquids and hydrocarbons, used for paving roads, and is known as black gold in the pavement industry. Currently, India meets nearly 50% of its bitumen requirement through imports. Innovations such as bio-bitumen can reduce import dependence while strengthening domestic production capabilities.
The process uses post-harvest rice straw as feedstock for producing bio-oil through pyrolysis.
The bio-oil is subsequently blended with conventional bitumen to produce the bio-bitumen blend. The technology uses biomass pyrolysis to produce multiple value streams, including bio-binders for roads, energy-efficient gaseous fuel, bio-pesticide fractions and high-grade carbon. These outputs have applications in batteries, water purification and advanced materials, offering an emission-free and cost-effective solution for the future.
A 100-metre trial stretch using bio-bitumen has been successfully laid on the Jorabat–Shillong Expressway (NH-40) in Meghalaya, demonstrating its feasibility. The technology also supports management of
farm residue.
Plans are underway to integrate this into national highway construction standards. With this, India has emerged as the first country to scale bio-bitumen technology to industrial and commercial levels within the same year.
The shift towards alternative materials is also visible in the wider use of recycled and industrial by-products in highway construction. Fly ash, a thermal power plant by-product, and pond ash are increasingly used in embankments and structural works.
Reclaimed Asphalt Pavement (RAP)
,
Construction and Demolition (C&D) waste and recycled aggregates
are also used in suitable highway works, as per technical specifications. Other materials being promoted include plastic waste, slag, crumb rubber, bio-bitumen and other recycled or industrial by-products. Together, these practices improve resource efficiency, conserve natural resources and help address environmental concerns associated with highway construction.
Community Engagement & Public Awareness
The impact of green highway initiatives is most visible on the ground, where plantations are being linked with biodiversity and community participation. Experiences from different States show how highway spaces can become platforms for wider environmental action.
Turning Highway Greenery into Pollinator Corridors
Green corridors along highways can serve purposes beyond shade and landscape improvement. Along identified stretches of the
Delhi-Amritsar-Katra Expressway
, pollinator corridors under the
“Trees for Bees”
campaign are being developed. The initiative uses flowering and locally suitable species to provide nectar and pollen across seasons, creating continuous habitat for bees and other pollinators.
Sustaining the Green Cover
Andhra Pradesh
has seen sustained plantation activity along its National Highway network. Between 2010 and 2025, around 18 lakh seedlings were planted through avenue and median plantations. These plantations are being maintained to mitigate the adverse impacts of climate change and ensure safer travel for highway users.
For 2026–27, a further 3.86 lakh saplings have been targeted for avenue and median plantation across the State. On World Environment Day 2026, around 3,200 saplings were planted across Andhra Pradesh under the
“Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam”
initiative.
Together, these efforts reflect a shift from planting trees along highways to nurturing green corridors that communities can help sustain over time.
Building the Highways of Tomorrow
India’s highway sector today stands at the intersection of large-scale infrastructure delivery and environmental stewardship. Each initiative, from grassroots plantation to indigenous bio-bitumen, reflects a common thread. Growth need not come at the expense of green cover. The Green Highways story is woven into India’s larger national priorities. These span climate action, self-reliance and inclusive growth. It reinforces the vision of Viksit Bharat through sustainable, technology-backed infrastructure. As India’s highway network expands, its green cover is expanding alongside it.

title: When Festivities Find a Greener Way to Celebrate
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                28 SEP 2026 4:09PM by PIB Delhi
content:
India's festivals arrive in many forms, but their emotional language is remarkably familiar. Ganesh Chaturthi brings Bappa into homes and neighbourhoods. Durga Puja fills pandals with devotion and artistry. Diwali brings the glow of diyas, prayers and new beginnings. Chhath brings families together at the ghats, offering prayers to the Sun. Rooted in faith, family and community, these celebrations are also closely tied to the spaces where they unfold.
A temple receives flowers, a pandal becomes a place of worship, and a ghat becomes part of a sacred ritual. As these traditions bring communities together, caring for these sacred spaces is becoming part of the celebration itself.  This spirit finds a national platform in
Swachhata Hi Seva 2026
, launched on
17 September 2026
. This year's campaign carries the theme
“Swachhata Mein Sahbhag; Swachh Bharat, Viksit Bharat”
. The campaign places shared responsibility for cleanliness at its heart, with
“Swachh Parv, Harit Parv”
focusing on clean and green festivities. It also promotes source segregation,
Reduce, Reuse and Recycle (3R’s)
, circular economy and
Waste-to-Wealth
initiatives.
Across India’s festive landscape, this idea is already finding expression in meaningful ways. Devotional flowers are being repurposed, clay is returning to Ganpati celebrations, bamboo is being used to create festive spaces, and Chhath ghats are being kept clean for devotees. Together, these efforts demonstrate how deeply rooted traditions can evolve with changing times while remaining anchored in faith, community participation, and a growing sense of environmental responsibility.
When Flowers of Devotion Find a New Life
At dawn in Ujjain, thousands of devotees enter the
Mahakaleshwar Temple
carrying flowers for worship. For them, the flowers are offerings of faith.  The temple receives around
75,000 to 100,000 visitors every day
and generates around
5 to 6 tonnes of floral waste daily
. Special
‘
Pushpanjali Econirmit’
vehicles collect the flowers and take them to a processing plant, where they are converted into products such as compost, briquettes and biofuels.
For the women of the
Shiv Arpan Self-Help Group
, discarded flowers have become a source of livelihood and renewed purpose. In 2024, by transforming floral waste into more than
30 million incense sticks
and other eco-friendly products, the initiative has turned waste into value while creating stable employment opportunities. In this way, a flower offered in devotion does not mark the end of its journey; after the prayer, it finds a new purpose through enterprise, livelihoods, and environmental responsibility.
When Celebration Meets Environmental Responsibility
For millions,
Ganesh Chaturthi
is a deeply personal celebration. Bappa enters homes amid music and prayers, becomes part of the family, and eventually departs for
visarjan
, carrying with him the promise of his return. The farewell is sacred, but it is also the moment when a cherished tradition intersects with the responsibility of protecting our water bodies.
In
2024, Navi Mumbai created 136 artificial ponds
for Ganesh idol immersion, providing devotees with designated spaces for
visarjan.
The locations were shared through social media and WhatsApp, making it easier for devotees to access these facilities while helping reduce pressure on natural water bodies.
The
Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC)
supplied around
500 tonnes of free clay
to sculptors, encouraging the use of traditional and environmentally conscious materials for Ganesh idols. Complementing this effort, the
Maharashtra Pollution Control Board
launched the
Eco-Bappa
mobile application to promote eco-friendly idols and decorations. The initiative encourages devotees and artisans to adopt sustainable practices while preserving the cultural and devotional essence of the celebration.
The idea also found resonance among young participants. The
Pimpri Chinchwad Municipal Corporation
organised an eco-friendly idol-making and decoration competition for students. They were encouraged to work with clay, papier-mâché, natural fibres and recycled materials, bringing environmental care into the celebrations. In Thane, Maharashtra, nearly
500 students
learnt to make Ganpati idols using
shadu
clay. Beyond developing their creativity and craftsmanship, these initiatives introduced young minds to the idea of carrying cherished traditions forward with greater environmental care.
Following the visarjan ceremony (2023), the spirit of participation continued. More than
900 Swachh volunteers
, including over
500 students
, helped clean Versova Beach. They removed around
80,000 kilograms of waste
and collected approximately
7,400 Plaster of Paris Ganesh idols
.
The farewell to Bappa became another opportunity for seva.
The green transformation does not always require something new. Sometimes, it means returning to materials that communities have known for generations.
In
Digboi, Assam
, Ganesh Puja (2023) was organised around bamboo. The material was used for idols, entrance gates, and traditional decorations, including the
Japi headgear and Khorahi baskets
. The celebration brought local tradition and environmental care together.
Delhi offered another expression of this idea through eco-friendly Ganesha idols made from
coconut bark and clay
, embedded with plantable seeds. After immersion, the idols dissolved into the soil, allowing the seeds to germinate and grow into plants. The ritual remains rooted in tradition, while the materials offer a
more sustainable way to complete the journey.
From Pandal to Prasad: A Greener Celebration
Durga Puja
is a celebration of devotion, artistry, and community, with pandals transforming into temporary spaces that welcome the goddess. Increasingly, the materials used to create these spaces reflect greater environmental awareness. In 2023, instead of thermocol and plastic,
bamboo, wood, coconut shells, cloth, jute, coir, hay, straw, cane, and paper
were used, while soluble clay Durga idols were also encouraged.
The effort extended beyond the pandal.
Blue and green waste bins
were placed at high-footfall locations, night-time cleanliness drives were organised, and non-plastic decorations were promoted. Some pandals in Delhi chose bamboo and cotton as the primary materials for their installations.
The offerings, too, found a second life.
Flowers and other organic materials
collected after the Puja were channelled towards composting and other productive uses. Prasad and refreshments were served on
paper plates, banana leaves, shell leaves and clay plates
, showing how familiar elements of the celebration can be retained while adopting more environmentally conscious practices.
Celebrating Diwali, Carrying the Spirit of Swachhata
Diwali has always been closely linked with cleanliness. Homes are cleaned, old things are sorted, and families come together for puja, gifts, and sweets. The
“Swachh Diwali, Shubh Diwali”
campaign builds on this tradition. It encourages waste segregation, the
3Rs- Reduce, Reuse, and Recycle
- locally made products, and cleaner celebrations.
In
Mira Bhayandar, Maharashtra
, the celebration began with preparation and community cleanliness. A special pre-Diwali sanitation drive saw Safai Mitras cleaning public spaces, washing statues of national heroes and freedom fighters, and tending to green areas.
In
Rajasthan and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands
, citizens are encouraged to take household waste generated during Diwali cleaning to nearby
Reduce, Reuse and Recycle centres
.
In 2023, the spirit of reuse also reached festive gifting. At the ‘
Swap Before You Shop-Gift Revival Mela’
in Delhi's Navjeevan Vihar, residents exchanged unused gifts through a categorised gift pool. 50 gifts were received in less than two hours on a single day.
Meanwhile, in
Melaghar, Tripura
, women from Self-Help Groups made earthen diyas for an eco-friendly Diwali. Further, Delhi's
Deep Mahotsav, Swachh Utsav and Voter Utsav
demonstrated how celebration itself could become a zero-waste experience. Fabric katran waste became reusable streamers, discarded cardboard became selfie frames, and old ice-cream sticks became hanging decorations. Their work kept a familiar tradition alive while offering a more sustainable choice.
After the Diyas Go Out
In
Guwahati
, the story continued even after the diyas were lit. Banana leaves used in the traditional Diwali celebration were collected afterwards and sent as feed for elephants.
In
Jhalrapatan, Rajasthan
,
Nirmalaya Vahan
vehicles collect garlands and other Puja material from temples. The collected material is then processed into compost. In
Indore, Madhya Pradesh
, special cleaning began as early as
4 am
after the festival. Under the
‘Clean Up to Clean Air’
initiative, sprinkler vehicles watered trees and plants with the message
‘Swachhata Se Swachh Vayu Ki Aur’
.
Where the River Becomes Part of the Prayer
Chhath
Puja
reflects one of India’s deeply rooted relationships with nature. Devotees offer prayers to the Sun while standing before the water, often along sacred rivers such as the
Ganga,
making the ghat an integral part of the ritual rather than merely a venue for the celebration.
In
Patna, Bihar
, the Municipal Corporation organises
zero-waste Chhath Puja
at designated ghats. Separate waste bins are installed, while dedicated vehicles collect waste generated during the celebrations. Wet waste is processed into organic compost, and a plastic ban is enforced. An extensive
Information, Education and Communication (IEC) campaign
is also conducted for a month ahead of the Puja to encourage devotees and the wider community to maintain a clean and hygienic festive environment.
The approach recognises that the sanctity of the festival is closely connected to the cleanliness of the spaces where it is observed.
When the river becomes part of worship, caring for its banks becomes an expression of reverence.
A Celebration That Leaves Something Good Behind
A festival is remembered for its prayers, lights, music, and the people who come together to celebrate. Yet every celebration also leaves something behind: a street to be cleaned, flowers at a ghat, an idol in a water body, or decorations left after the crowds have dispersed. Increasingly, it can leave something more:
a cleaner ghat, a recycled decoration, a clay idol, a new plant, a livelihood, or a community that has learnt to celebrate with greater care.
India’s festivals do not need to lose their colour to become greener. The diya can still glow, the drums can still play, and prayers can still rise. What can change is what we leave behind when the celebration ends.
A celebration is truly complete when its joy remains with people, while its burden does not remain with the earth.

title: Beyond the Fab
subtitle: How Dholera Is Building the Ecosystem Around India’s Semiconductor Ambition
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                28 SEP 2026 3:53PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Setting the Context
A semiconductor manufacturing facility is only one part of what it takes to build a semiconductor hub. Behind the clean rooms, advanced equipment and production lines lies a wider ecosystem of hospitals, schools, housing, emergency services and commercial infrastructure that enables companies and their workforce to operate over the long term.
At Dholera in Gujarat, this broader ecosystem is taking shape alongside the development of the semiconductor manufacturing cluster.
Gujarat has emerged as a major centre of India’s semiconductor expansion, with
six of the 12 semiconductor manufacturing projects approved under Semicon India 1.0
located in the State. The projects, with cumulative investment commitments of more than
₹
1.64 lakh crore
nationally, span semiconductor fabrication, compound semiconductor and display technologies, and advanced packaging.
The scale of these investments is also driving a parallel development: the creation of an industrial township equipped to support the people and businesses that will become part of the semiconductor ecosystem.
During a panel discussion on Investment Facilitation and Ease of Doing Business at SEMICON India 2026, Neha Kumari, IAS, Mission Director, Gujarat State Electronics Mission (GSEM), Gandhinagar, outlined how Dholera is building this supporting infrastructure alongside the industrial cluster.
Building what comes after the fab
Building what comes after the fab
Healthcare is among the key components of this ecosystem. A 200-bed hospital is under construction at Dholera, with completion targeted by December 2026. The facility is expected to be managed by the Government of Gujarat. Alongside the physical infrastructure, work is also underway on emergency Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) and coordination mechanisms with relevant agencies.
Education is another important element. A school following the International Baccalaureate (IB) curriculum is being developed in the township. The building is ready, with the project targeted for completion around October 2026. Discussions are also underway with private players for operating the school.
For professionals and investors working in the emerging industrial cluster, accommodation is being developed as well. A dedicated investor accommodation facility is targeted for completion by September-end 2026, adding to the township’s capacity to host people working in the region.
Other civic infrastructure is progressing in parallel. A fire station has been completed, while a food court was completed in July 2026. Residential and commercial developments are also underway, with completion projected between mid-2027 and the end of 2027.
A Tent City has been completed, with vendors in the final stages of obtaining approvals to begin operations, while a hotel is currently under construction.
From industrial project to industrial ecosystem
The developments point to a broader shift in how large industrial investments are being planned. A semiconductor facility requires not only sophisticated manufacturing infrastructure but also an environment that can support a specialised workforce and the families that accompany it.
For Dholera, this means developing the social and physical infrastructure around the industrial cluster at the same time as manufacturing capabilities are being established.
Significant activity has been taking place on the ground over the past
one-and-a-half to two years
, reflecting the pace at which Dholera’s supporting infrastructure is being developed alongside the semiconductor project.
The implication of this approach extends beyond individual facilities. Hospitals provide healthcare, schools support families, accommodation serves incoming professionals and investors, while emergency and commercial infrastructure contributes to the functioning of an industrial township.
With
six semiconductor manufacturing projects
located in Gujarat, the State is becoming an important part of India’s semiconductor manufacturing journey. At Dholera, that journey is being accompanied by the creation of the ecosystem around the factory floor.
The emerging model is therefore about more than building a semiconductor fab. It is about creating an integrated industrial destination - one where manufacturing, infrastructure and everyday life can develop together, providing the foundation needed to support India’s semiconductor ambitions at scale.

title: Pradhan Mantri Anusuchit Jaati Abhyuday Yojna (PM-AJAY)
subtitle: Building Pathways to Progress
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                28 SEP 2026 11:57AM by PIB Delhi
content:
Scheduled Castes (SCs), constituting 16.6% of India's population, have historically faced barriers to socio-economic advancement and inclusion. Addressing these disparities is vital to ensuring social justice, equal opportunity, and broader participation in India's development journey
.
Recognising these development gaps, the Government of India launched Pradhan Mantri Anusuchit Jaati Abhyuday Yojana (PM-AJAY) to foster the overall development of Scheduled Castes.
A Vision for Inclusive Empowerment
The
Pradhan Mantri Anusuchit Jaati Abhyuday Yojna (PM-AJAY)
is a 100% centrally sponsored scheme launched in FY 2021-22. It envisions achieving socio-economic and educational empowerment of Scheduled Caste communities through a comprehensive and integrated approach.
The Government has launched
‘PM-AJAY’ Mobile App
and
‘PM-AJAY’ Portal
for expedited and quality implementation of the PM-AJAY Scheme.
PM-AJAY
is a
merger scheme
of three erstwhile centrally sponsored schemes, namely,
Pradhan Mantri Adarsh Gram Yojana (PMAGY)
,
Special Central Assistance to Scheduled Castes Sub Plan (SCA to SCSP)
and
Babu Jagjivan Ram Chhatrawas Yojana (BJRCY)
. Implemented by the
Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment,
PM-AJAY turns its broader goal of ensuring development for everyone into practical action through the following three main objectives:
To reduce poverty of the SC communities by generation of additional employment opportunities. It can be done through skill development, income generating schemes and other initiatives. These interventions seek to enhance livelihood opportunities and enable beneficiaries to engage in sustainable income-generating activities.
To improve socio-economic developmental indicators by ensuring adequate infrastructure and requisite services in SC dominated areas. The scheme seeks to bridge critical developmental gaps and improve access to essential facilities that contribute to a better quality of life.
To increase literacy and encourage enrolment of SCs in schools and higher educational institutions. It is achieved by providing adequate residential facilities in quality institutions and residential schools, especially in aspirational districts/SC-dominated blocks and elsewhere in India.
Who Can Benefit from PM-AJAY?
At the heart of PM-AJAY lies a carefully defined framework of eligibility, ensuring that the benefits of the scheme reach the individuals and communities for whom they are intended. Accordingly, access to the scheme is determined on the basis of the following criteria:
While selecting beneficiaries under GIA component, priority is given to the families/persons having annual income not more than Rs. 2.50 lakh per annum. SC members of SC majority group are also be eligible.
In case of Infrastructure Development, villages having 40% or more SC population and total population more than or equal to 500 are eligible for grants under the Scheme.
PM-AJAY in Action
The architecture of PM-AJAY rests on three distinct components to address various aspects of development:
Development of SC dominated villages into “Adarsh Gram”
Transforming SC-majority villages into
‘Adarsh Grams’
(model villages) by filling critical gaps in infrastructure and services. ​ The
Adarsh Gram component
has covered
47,243 villages
, benefiting more than
47.79 lakh citizens
across the country. A total of
46,944 development works
have been completed, while
27,032 Village Development Plans (VDPs)
have been prepared. As on 8th September 2026,
18,093 villages
have been declared as
Adarsh Grams
, reflecting significant progress in improving infrastructure, basic services and quality of life in Scheduled Caste-majority villages.
An ‘Adarsh Gram’ is one wherein people have access to various basic services. The minimum needs of all the sections of the society are fully met and disparities are reduced to a minimum. These villages are envisioned to have all essential infrastructure and universal access to basic services required for dignified living. This creates an enabling environment for every resident to realise their full potential.
Grants-in-aid for Socio-Economic Projects to State/Districts
Providing financial assistance for district/state-level projects aimed at the socio-economic betterment of SCs. This includes:​
Increasing the income of the target population by way of comprehensive livelihood projects, including skill development and related infrastructure.
Improving socio-economic developmental indicators by creating adequate infrastructure in SC dominated villages.
Increasing literacy and encouraging enrolment of SCs in schools by providing residential schools where required.
More than
₹
1,730 crore
has been released directly to States under the Grants-in-Aid component from FY 2021-22 to FY 2025-26. It extends skilling and livelihood support to over
2.5 lakh individual and group beneficiaries
.
Construction/Repair of Hostels
The construction and repair of hostels is one of the means to enable and encourage students belonging to Scheduled Castes (SC) to attain quality education. Such hostels are immensely beneficial to the students hailing from rural and remote areas of the country. As of
September 2026
, a
total of
785 student hostels have been completed.
The Government has allocated central assistance of
₹
61.46 crore
for
FY 2026-27
for construction of
two hostel projects
(one for girls and one for boys)
to provide accommodation for
264
students.
Investing in Empowerment
Effective implementation of any welfare initiative requires sustained financial support. An overview of the funding framework under PM-AJAY is presented below.
Funding at a Glance
Funding Pattern
100% Centrally Funded Scheme
State/UT Contribution
States/UTs may supplement the scheme with additional resources, if required
Component-wise Allocation
Up to 50%
- Gap-filling activities in selected
Adarsh Gram
villages.
Up to 5%
- For setting up and operation of the TSG (Technical Support Group) and PIU (Project Implementation Units) at the Central level as well as PIU at the State and District level.
Up to 2%
– Construction and repair of hostels- to be utilized for Central Institutions and released directly to the implementing agencies by the Ministry.
Remaining funds
- Grants-in-aids for the Projects at District/State, allocated based on Scheduled Caste population and ratio of State SCSP to the Annual Plan as compared to the SC population in the States/UTs.
Maintenance
Post completion of the infrastructure projects under the scheme, their upkeep and operations shall be taken care of by the State Governments/implementing agencies, as the case may be.
A Digital Leap Towards Effective Governance
The recent launch of the
‘PM-AJAY’ Mobile App
and
‘PM-AJAY’ Portal
aims to transition from paper-based workflow and processing to an end-to-end digital workflow and processing on a real-time basis.
Good governance is built on the principles of transparency, accountability and efficiency.
Digital technologies have transformed the planning, delivery and monitoring of public programmes. Technology-enabled governance improves information access, strengthens monitoring and supports data-driven decision-making. It also enhances coordination, transparency and the overall effectiveness of
programme implementation.
The Next Chapter in India’s Growth Story
The journey towards
Viksit Bharat @2047
is founded on the principle that the benefits of development must reach every section of society and create opportunities for all to progress. In this endeavour,
PM-AJAY
plays a significant role in advancing the socio-economic and educational empowerment of Scheduled Caste communities through targeted interventions that promote sustainable livelihoods, quality education and improved infrastructure. As the scheme continues to expand, greater use of technology, stronger monitoring mechanisms, and focused last-mile delivery are enhancing its effectiveness and outreach. By empowering individuals and communities to realise their full potential and actively participate in India's development journey, PM-AJAY will continue to foster a more inclusive, equitable, and empowered nation.
